stories.headline: Russia Sentences Last Registered Anti-War Politician to 11 Years, Bans His Party from September Elections
stories.summary:
A Russian court in Pskov sentenced Lev Shlosberg, the deputy head of the liberal Yabloko party and the country's most prominent remaining anti-war politician, to 11 years and one month in a penal colony on Monday. He was convicted of "discrediting" Russia's armed forces and "spreading false information" about them, charges stemming from social media posts. The verdict was handed down minutes before Russia's Supreme Court separately rejected Yabloko's appeal against a ban on participating in September's parliamentary elections.

Shlosberg, 63, condemned the ruling as politically motivated, telling the court its only purpose was to "punish a person for his political, public and civil position." He was repeatedly interrupted by the presiding judge during his closing statement, in which he again called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and political dialogue. Yabloko said it would appeal the sentence.

Yabloko was the only registered Russian party to oppose the full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched in 2022. Its exclusion from September's elections—justified by authorities on grounds including alleged support for the "international LGBT movement" and copyright infringement—leaves all 10 remaining parties on the ballot as supporters of the war. Independent election watchdogs have been largely stripped of their ability to monitor the process.

The sentencing marks a significant escalation in the Kremlin's suppression of domestic dissent ahead of the September 18-20 parliamentary vote. Shlosberg's imprisonment removes the last prominent legal opposition voice inside Russia, reinforcing the wartime censorship apparatus that has effectively criminalized public criticism of the military campaign in Ukraine.

stories.headline: Lake Powell Hits Record Low, Threatening Water and Power for 40 Million in Seven States
stories.summary:
Lake Powell, the United States' second-largest reservoir, dropped to a record low elevation of 3,519.91 feet above sea level on Saturday, edging below the previous record set in April 2023. The milestone comes roughly a week after the Colorado River's other major reservoir, Lake Mead, also hit a historic low. Together, the two reservoirs now hold less combined water than at any point since the Glen Canyon Dam was under construction in May 1957.

The Colorado River Basin is the primary water source for more than 40 million people across seven states—California, Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and Colorado—and supports significant hydroelectric power generation. Lake Powell is now approximately 30 feet above the elevation at which its turbines would stop producing electricity. Federal officials warned in April that a "major intervention" would be needed to avoid that threshold by year's end.

Persistent overuse of the river, a record-dry winter, and rising temperatures have driven the depletion. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation proposed a 10-year management plan in July that includes potentially significant water cuts for Arizona, California and Nevada, but the federal government and the seven basin states have yet to reach agreement on a long-term framework.

The crisis is already affecting Lake Powell's tourism economy, forcing marina relocations, closure of boat ramps, and adaptation across the recreational industry. Scientists and retired water officials who published a recent analysis of the combined reservoir data say levels may continue to fall, making a negotiated solution increasingly urgent.

stories.headline: Record Rainfall Triggers Fatal Landslide in South Korea as Storms Batter East Asia
stories.summary:
A landslide struck an apartment building in the South Korean city of Geoje on Monday morning following record-breaking rainfall, killing one person and injuring two others. Rescuers pulled three residents from the buried ground floor of the building. Geoje recorded 124.5mm of rainfall in a single hour—the highest one-hour total since meteorological records for the city began in 1972—with more than 400mm falling overnight between Sunday and Monday.

The disaster is part of a broader pattern of extreme weather striking East and Southeast Asia this month. Back-to-back storms have caused widespread flooding and landslides across South Korea, China, Japan and the Philippines. Japan's Chiba prefecture near Tokyo recorded "unprecedented" rainfall last week that killed 10 people, stranded thousands at Narita Airport and cut power to more than 20,000 households. Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in eastern China on Monday, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to Shanghai and surrounding areas.

Forecasters attribute the unusually intense typhoon season to a strong El Niño pattern that began in June, which raises global temperatures and increases the destructive power of typhoons. Multiple storms sweeping through the region in rapid succession have strained emergency response capacity and damaged infrastructure across several countries simultaneously.

South Korean city authorities have closed tourist attractions in Geoje and suspended bus operations and waste collection due to flooded or damaged roads. Residents were urged on Sunday to avoid driving and stay away from riverbanks as further rain continues to threaten the region.

stories.headline: UK Prime Minister Burnham Exchanged Messages With Impersonator Posing as Trump's Chief of Staff Susie Wiles
stories.summary:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham communicated with an unknown individual impersonating Susie Wiles, White House chief of staff and one of President Trump's closest advisers, according to people familiar with the matter. The incident raises immediate national security concerns about the new prime minister's communications protocols and vetting procedures for high-level contacts.

Four outlets including Bloomberg, CBS News, the New York Post, and The Guardian are covering the story. Accounts differ slightly in tone: the Guardian described the suspicious activity as having been identified quickly with no messages of significance exchanged, while the New York Post characterized it as Burnham stumbling into a national security gaffe shortly after taking office.

The episode is politically embarrassing for Burnham's government at a sensitive moment in UK-US relations, particularly as Britain navigates diplomacy with the Trump administration. It is not yet clear who was behind the impersonation, what the perpetrator's motive was, or how the suspicious contact was ultimately flagged and terminated.

stories.headline: Fed Minutes, Walmart and Home Depot Earnings headline a Major Week for Wall Street Amid Persistent Inflation
stories.summary:
Wall Street faces a consequential week with earnings reports from four of the nation's largest retailers — Home Depot on Tuesday, Target and Lowe's on Wednesday, and Walmart on Thursday — along with the release of minutes from the Federal Reserve's most recent policy meeting on Wednesday. Investors and economists are watching the results closely for signals about how businesses and consumers are coping with inflation that remains solidly above 3 percent.

The ongoing U.S. war with Iran has driven a surge in oil prices, pushing up gasoline costs and raising prices on a wide range of goods. Results from home improvement retailers could shed light on housing market conditions, while Walmart and Target figures will offer a clearer picture of household budgeting and discretionary spending under sustained price pressure.

The Fed held interest rates steady at its July meeting, though three officials dissented in favor of higher rates — a rift Fed Chair Kevin Warsh publicly called a 'good family fight.' Wall Street currently anticipates at least one rate hike before year's end, and the release of meeting minutes may clarify how close policymakers are to pulling that trigger.

stories.headline: What Happens to the Personal Information You Share With AI Chatbots
stories.summary:
A new Axios investigation examines the largely unregulated landscape governing how artificial intelligence companies handle sensitive personal information shared by users during chatbot conversations. The report highlights a scenario with few legal guardrails: a chatbot designed to maximize engagement or influence purchasing decisions could potentially draw on fears, insecurities, and private disclosures a user has shared to tailor its responses.

The investigation focuses on the promises made by major AI companies — including OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Anthropic — about consumer data use, noting that those promises carry outsized weight precisely because formal regulatory requirements remain sparse. Questions about data retention, secondary use of personal disclosures, and whether AI systems can leverage intimate user information for commercial ends are at the center of the inquiry.

The story comes as concern grows among educators, policymakers, and consumer advocates about AI's rapid integration into daily life. Separately, the New York Times is also reporting on the issue, indicating growing mainstream attention to the gap between AI companies' self-described data policies and what users actually understand about the fate of what they share.

stories.headline: Update: Indonesia Earthquake Death Toll Rises to 68 as Aid Shortages and Starvation Fears Mount in Flores
stories.summary:
A 7.7-magnitude earthquake that struck the Indonesian island of Flores on Saturday has now killed at least 68 people and displaced approximately 5,000, making it the country's deadliest quake since 2022. Landslides have severed access roads to the hardest-hit villages, cutting off survivors from rescue teams, food, and medical supplies. Thousands remain sleeping outdoors in makeshift shelters, fearing further collapses as aftershocks continue to rattle the region.

The acute shortage of medical personnel has emerged as a critical crisis. Dr. Melinda, the sole physician at the decimated Dampek Health Centre, posted an urgent appeal describing herself as unable to cope with hundreds of casualties arriving around the clock without rest. Ruteng Regional General Hospital, roughly four hours from the worst-hit areas, has also reported that promised medical assistance had not yet arrived.

More than 1,000 houses were damaged, along with dozens of health facilities, schools, and government offices, according to Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency. Search-and-rescue teams are still working to reach cut-off communities, and officials warn the full casualty count may not yet be known. The death toll has risen from the 53 previously reported, representing a material new development in an ongoing disaster.

stories.headline: Hurricane Lala Sweeps Away About 100 Homes in Hawaii, Knocks Out Power to 219,000
stories.summary:
Hurricane Lala skirted the Big Island of Hawaii on Saturday and Sunday, delivering catastrophic flash flooding and mudslides without making direct landfall. Roughly 100 or more homes were uprooted from their foundations by torrents of water, and more than 219,000 households lost electricity. Three hospitals also lost power, though backup generators kept them operational. Governor Josh Green said there were, 'amazingly,' no confirmed fatalities linked directly to the home destruction, though one person died in a car accident.

The storm dumped as much as 32 inches of rain in some areas, with its eyewall passing within 30 miles of South Point overnight. Wind speeds peaked at 91 mph before Lala weakened to a tropical storm tracking westward, south of the islands. Tropical storm warnings remained in effect for all eight of Hawaii's major islands on Sunday, and the governor deployed approximately 180 National Guard members to assist with emergency response.

Both of Big Island's main airports — Hilo International and Ellison Onizuka Kona — were temporarily closed, with some 190 flights postponed. Maui residents faced water supply disruptions. Hawaii has not seen a hurricane make landfall since Category 4 Hurricane Iniki struck Kauai in 1992, causing six deaths and $3 billion in damage. Officials warned the danger was not yet over as the storm continued to track near the island chain.

stories.headline: Zambian Security Forces Raid Opposition Leader's Home on Election Day After Shootout
stories.summary:
Zambian security forces raided the residence of the country's main opposition leader on the day of the presidential election, arresting 11 people following a shootout. Authorities described the operation as part of an investigation into an alleged plot involving foreign nationals. The incident drew immediate scrutiny from international observers monitoring the election.

President Hakainde Hichilema appeared on course for an outright re-election victory, according to early reports, but election observers noted violence and what they characterized as a tilted campaign environment. The raid on the opposition leader's home on election day raised concerns about political interference and the integrity of the democratic process in one of southern Africa's historically more stable democracies.

Zambia has been regarded as a regional model for peaceful transfers of power since its independence era, making the armed raid and shootout at an opposition leader's compound during voting a significant and alarming development. International observers and regional bodies had been monitoring the election, and their assessments of the pre-election environment and the day's events are expected to shape the international response to the outcome.

stories.headline: Actress Hayden Panettiere, Star of 'Nashville' and 'Heroes,' Dies at 36
stories.summary:
Hayden Panettiere, the actress best known for her roles as cheerleader Claire Bennet in the NBC series 'Heroes' and country music star Juliette Barnes in 'Nashville,' has died at age 36. Her representative confirmed the death to ABC News. Panettiere had worked in entertainment since infancy, appearing in commercials at 11 months old, and built a long career as a child and adult actress.

In May 2026, Panettiere published a memoir chronicling a turbulent decade that included battles with depression and substance abuse, stints in rehabilitation, and losing custody of her daughter Kaya, whom she shares with former fiancé and professional boxer Wladimir Klitschko. She had spoken publicly in recent years about her struggles and her efforts toward recovery. Tributes from the entertainment industry poured in following the announcement of her death.

Panettiere's death was reported by seven major outlets, making it one of the most widely covered stories of the day. She was 36 years old.
